sentences.text: Pelagornis is an extinct genus of pseudotooth birds, a group now primarily known by the family name Pelagornithidae.
These birds possessed tooth-like or knob-like extensions on their bills called pseudo-teeth to help grip slippery prey, structures that lacked enamel and did not grow in sockets.
Unlike Osteodontornis, Pelagornis featured a single smaller pseudo-tooth between each pair of large pseudo-teeth, similar to the older Pseudodontornis.
Pelagornis possessed extremely large and well-developed salt glands located inside its eye sockets.
Pelagornis sandersi holds the record for the widest wingspan of any bird known, approximately twice that of the modern wandering albatross.
It is estimated that P. sandersi could fly at speeds of up to 60 km/h.
Pelagornis sandersi is named after Albert Sanders, who led the excavation of the fossil.
The genus Pelagornis was described by Lartet in 1857.
The genus is divided into four species: P. chilensis (Mayr & Rubilar, 2010), P. mauretanicus (Mourer-Chauviré & Geraads, 2008), P. miocaenus (Lartet, 1857), and P. sandersi (Ksepka, 2014).
The type species Pelagornis miocaenus is known from 23 million-year-old sediments.
The species Pelagornis mauretanicus was named in 2008, with remains found in 2.5 million-year-old deposits in Morocco.

Goedert et al. (2026) reported the discovery of a Pelagornis orri braincase from the Miocene Astoria Formation in Oregon and isolated bones from the Eocene Keasey Formation, representing one of the oldest pelagornithid records.
Due to its large size, P. sandersi likely moulted all of its flight feathers simultaneously, a behavior similar to ducks, geese, or grebes.
Pelagornis was not a skim-feeder because it could not generate enough energy to overcome the drag required for skimming prey from the ocean surface.
P. sandersi had short, stumpy legs and likely flew by hopping off cliff edges rather than taking off from flat ground.
Pelagornis was initially thought to be related to albatrosses but is now classified in the Pelecaniformes.
Pelagornis fossils date from the Late Oligocene to the Early Pleistocene, spanning from 25 to 2.5 million years ago.
The genus Pelagornis existed from the Bartonian to the Piacenzian, between 41.03 and 2.58 million years ago.

Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in the Eocene Aridal Formation in Morocco and the La Meseta Formation on Seymour Island, Antarctica, the Oligocene Chandler Bridge Formation in South Carolina, USA, and Miocene deposits across Australia, Chile, France, the USA, New Zealand, Peru, Portugal, and Venezuela.

There was originally a scientific debate regarding whether P. sandersi was capable of flight, as its weight of 21.9 to 40.1 kg exceeded the limits predicted by predominant theories of bird flight mechanics.
Researchers suggest Pacific fossils may represent a species distinct from P. miocaenus or closer to Osteodontornis.
It is debated whether Pseudodontornis belongs to a distinct lineage, which might require revalidating the family name Pseudodontornithidae.
Research published in 2026 by Hellyer-Price, Venditti, and Humphries argues that Pelagornis was likely unable to skim-feed based on drag calculations.
